findings.claim: Neither findHeredocs nor tokenizeShell recognized a `#` comment, so an apostrophe inside a comment opened a single-quoted region to the end of the command and hid every later heredoc and program position — the charter's flagship positive control slipped through (POSIX 2.3 rule 10; bash §3.1.3: a comment is discarded without quote processing).
findings.counterexample:
`# don't clobber the file
cat > f.mjs <<'EOF'
const re = /\d+/;
EOF` — expected deny(heredoc-escape) per the mmnto-ai/totem#2799 positive control; actual allow, 0 spans. Same carrier blinded sed-i-escape and msys-body-slash; a trailing comment (`echo hi # don't`) did the same.

findings.claim: sed-i-escape's newline test read seg.raw, which still held an unquoted backslash-newline continuation, so a benign wrapped `sed -i` was denied against the tokenizer's own comment, bash §3.1.2.1, the changeset's 'quoted newline' scope and the ADR-109 zero budget.
findings.counterexample: `grep -q x f && \\\n  sed -i 's/foo/bar/' file.ts` — expected allow; actual deny 'a sed -i invocation spans a newline'. The one-line and newline-separated forms allowed, so the continuation alone caused it.

findings.claim: `<<` inside an arithmetic expansion was read as a heredoc operator whenever its right operand was an identifier, creating a phantom heredoc whose body was every later line — blanked for the other rows (fail-open) and scanned for escapes (spurious deny).
findings.counterexample: `mask=$((1 << n))\ngh pr comment 5 -b /gemini` (win32) — expected deny(msys-body-slash); actual allow. `mask=$((1 << n))\nsed -i 's/a/b/' 'C:\\x\\y.txt'` — expected allow; actual deny(heredoc-escape).

findings.claim: HEREDOC_AT accepted only quote characters around the delimiter, so the backslash-quoted spelling `<<\EOF` (POSIX 2.7.4: any quoted character in the word quotes the delimiter) was not a heredoc — its body missed by heredoc-escape and scanned as shell text.
findings.counterexample:
`cat > f <<\EOF
const re = /\d+/;
EOF` — expected deny(heredoc-escape); actual allow. `cat > f <<\EOF
gh pr comment 5 -b /some/path
EOF` (win32) — expected allow; actual deny(msys-body-slash).

findings.claim: tokenizeShell treated a word-initial `#` as an ordinary character, so comment text was tokenized as arguments and could satisfy a deny row (ADR-109 budget: zero denies over benign commands).
findings.counterexample: `gh pr comment 5 --body-file notes.md # was --body /gemini review` (win32) — expected allow; actual deny(msys-body-slash). `sed -i -e 's/a/b/' f.txt # -e 's/c/d/'` — expected allow; actual deny (2 -e expressions).

findings.claim: The wrapper passed the whole Bash command as one argv element, so on win32 a command past the 32,767-character limit failed the spawn with ENAMETOOLONG and landed in the fail-closed arm ('source broken or unavailable') with nothing broken and no cure — the spec's failure-mode table reserves that arm for a broken source.
findings.counterexample: Measured on win32 (node v24): spawnSync with a 40,000-character argument → error.code ENAMETOOLONG; 32,000 → ok. Expected per the table: a verdict or a not-applicable exit 0; actual exit 2.

findings.claim: programIndex skipped assignments before wrappers only, so the canonical `env VAR=VALUE prog` never reached the program; a `&`-backgrounded first command hid the second; wrappers with operands (`sudo -u me`, `timeout 30`, `npx`) defeat the anchor.
findings.counterexample: `env GH_TOKEN=x gh pr comment 5 -b /x` (win32) — expected deny(msys-body-slash); actual allow. `sleep 1 & gh pr comment 5 -b /x` — the same.

findings.claim: optionAsWritten returned on the FIRST `--body`/`-b` token even when it was another option's value, so a later real `--body` was never examined.
findings.counterexample: `gh issue create --title -b --body /x` (win32) — expected deny(msys-body-slash); actual allow.

findings.claim: The header's comment rule cites bash, but the evaluator also runs for tool PowerShell, whose block comment `<# … #>` is not recognized — an apostrophe inside one can still desynchronize the quote scan for that tool; pre-existing and undisclosed.
findings.counterexample: tool PowerShell, `<# don't #>\nsed -i 's/\t/ /' f` — expected deny(sed-i-escape); actual allow.

findings.claim: The re-armed fold's disclosure 'a `#` directly after a subshell's closing `)` is over-scan, never a miss' was false: dropping `)` from WORD_BOUNDARY made findHeredocs read a `#` after an OPERATOR `)` (a subshell's, a case pattern's) as word text, where POSIX 2.3 rule 6 delimits the `)` as an operator and rule 9 makes the `#` a comment — an apostrophe in that comment then desynchronized the quote scan and hid a later heredoc (a fold-introduced miss with a false-deny mirror). Only the `)` closing a `$( … )` is part of a word (rule 5).
findings.counterexample:
`(echo a)#it's a note
cat <<'EOF'
x\d
EOF` — bash 5.3.15 prints `a` then `x\d` (comment discarded, heredoc runs); expected deny(heredoc-escape), 400bac3a denied, f0eb6f12 allowed. Mirror: `(echo a)#see <<'EOF'
x\d
EOF` — bash has no heredoc; f0eb6f12 denied.

findings.claim: The new HEREDOC_AT comment claimed an unread delimiter (`<<1`, `<<$X`) was 'a disclosed gap, over-scan direction only'; an unread heredoc operator leaves its BODY to be scanned as shell text, so an apostrophe there opens a quote region and hides a later, real heredoc — the miss direction. The pre-existing behaviour was out of scope; the claim was new.
findings.counterexample:
`cat <<1EOF
it's
1EOF
cat <<'EOF'
x\d
EOF` — bash prints `it's` then `x\d`; expected deny(heredoc-escape); actual at f0eb6f12 allow, 0 spans.

findings.claim: The WORD_BOUNDARY comment cited POSIX 2.3 rule 10 for the comment rule and rule 9 for word continuation; the comment rule is 9 and word continuation is 8.
findings.counterexample: POSIX.1-2017 XCU 2.3: rule 8 appends to an open word, rule 9 discards a `#` comment, rule 10 starts a new word.

findings.claim: Three new sub-assertions do not discriminate the re-armed fold (the tokenizer `$(true)#x` shape, the `echo 'a' $( … )` warn row, the `awk -F\'` benign row); each parent test still discriminates, so no false green.
findings.counterexample: Measured against a byte-verified reconstruction of the 400bac3a evaluator: identical results on both shas for those three sub-assertions.

findings.claim: The HEREDOC_AT comment disclosed a literal `$X` delimiter as 'the over-scan direction' — bash does not expand a heredoc delimiter word either, so the scanner and bash terminate at the same literal line and there was no divergence to disclose (echoed in the changeset and the spec). Safe-direction over-disclosure.
findings.counterexample:
`cat <<$X
b
EOF
$X
z` — the comment expected an unterminated body; findHeredocs terminated at the literal `$X` line and bash (script s1.sh) printed `b`, `EOF`, `done` — the same.

findings.claim: POSIX 2.3 rule 5 was cited to justify `<( … )` continuing a word; rule 5 enumerates only the `$` and backquote introducers — process substitution is a bash extension (§3.5.6). The behaviour is correct; the citation over-reached.
findings.counterexample: `echo <(echo a)#y` — bash prints `/dev/fd/63#y`, one word (script b1.sh); the grounding is bash's own behaviour, not rule 5.

findings.claim: Five of the thirteen new sub-assertions and two of the three new budget rows do not discriminate against the f0eb6f12 evaluator (guards, not falsifiers); both new parent tests and both budget tests still fail on the pre-fold code.
findings.counterexample: Identical results on both shas for the `$(a)# it's` and `<(…)#it's` span checks, the `1EOF … sed` allow, the `x=$(cat <<EOF)` and `cat <<EOF;` delimiter reads, and the last two budget rows.
